also: a stone’s throw from the sea

terms.gloss: a spear’s throw: a very short distance
terms.grammar: intrā tēlī jactum, “within a spear’s throw”; tēlī jactū abesse, “be a spear’s throw away”
evidence: Verg. A. 11.608: jamque intrā jactum tēlī prōgressus uterque substiterat
Liv. 8.7: ita ut vix tēlī jactū ab statiōne proximā abesset
terms.comment: Where English throws a stone, the Roman authors measure a short distance by the throw of a spear; the phrase is at home in battle narrative. Livy also says tēlī conjectus in the same sense, and of a peaceful thing: Scipio camped where there was water intrā tēlī conjectum (30.29).

evidence: Apul. Flor. 2: nec cernere nōs nisi intrā lapidis jactum valēre
terms.comment: Apuleius’s phrase, the image English uses: that our eyes reach no further than a stone’s throw.

phrases.latin: Fōns vix tēlī jactū abest; licet tibi praecurrere.
phrases.english: The fountain is only a stone’s throw away; you may run on ahead.

phrases.latin: Domus avī vix lapidis jactū ā marī abest.
phrases.english: Grandpa’s house is a stone’s throw from the sea.

phrases.latin: jamque intrā jactum tēlī prōgressus uterque substiterat
phrases.english: and now each side had advanced to within a spear’s throw and halted

phrases.latin: quod aquātiō intrā tēlī conjectum erat
phrases.english: because there was water within a spear’s throw

sources: Lewis & Short: jactus · Lewis & Short: conjectus
